baseline: The toy 3D slider labels weights as glasses, lipstick and young with the full sphere, while the paper's stated default of θ=φ=π/2 is presented as activating all attributes without noting that it conflicts with Eq. 4 (mild).

Claims all numbers on the page are taken from Table 1, but the toy angular panel presents Old and Smiling as the circle attributes, whereas the paper's Fig. 1 uses Old and Asian (labeled as a toy, so minor).
The 3D sphere toy labels the three attributes as glasses, lipstick and young with specific axes; this is an illustration, not something the paper specifies.

The mask toy follows the main text's reading of q, where a higher threshold gives a tighter mask, although the page also notes that the Fig. 5 caption says the opposite; the paper is internally inconsistent here.
candidate: Claims a combined push of about 1.41x for two full sliders and that the total push stays at 1 for orthogonal arrows; this is the page's own derivation, not stated in the paper.

The footer asserts that Fig. 4 lets Cyprus act as a prompt for a group of people and that SphereEdit's lipstick in Fig. 3 is faint, which are the page's own readings of the figures, not claims the paper makes.

The page says the paper notes the mask direction q is ambiguous between caption and text; this is accurate, but the statement that two of four rival editors shift the whole photo's colour is a slight narrowing of the paper's claim that Composable Diffusion and TurboEdit introduce global tone shifts.
